questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Academic opportunities

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer: I chose UNIS on Svalbard due to my academic interests and because I wanted to find a relevant destination leading up to my master thesis

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: I went on exchange due to academic interests, but it ended up being the outdoor and social experiences that made it a great stay rather than the courses

questions.question: How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: Easy in general, but I still felt super confused and felt like everyone else knew more than me

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: There was an introduction week at UNIS

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
questions.answer: Most of the information came on monday morning when the introduction week started, but until then you felt very confused

questions.question: How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing through my host institution

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: On campus

questions.question: What options were available for on campus housing? *
questions.answer: There was a student dorm where everyone lives (Elvesletta, 5 min walk from UNIS)

questions.question: What options were available for meal plans or cooking facilities? *
questions.answer: Great facilities. I lived in a single room with common kitchen. The kitchen had freezer, fridge, stove and microwave. Nothing else than that, so no kettle, coffee machine or toaster

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about on campus housing? *
questions.answer: It is socially intense and maybe a bit overwhelming. But I would really recommend to have a shared kitchen, because this gives a lot of social support and a feeling of safety/comfort.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer:
I had to register at a Norwegian university, and then figure out registering for courses at Svalbard on my own. 

It felt super uncertain because UNIS does not have a possibility to sign up for a full semester as a master student (this is possible for bachelor exchange students). So I had to apply for courses seperately and then just hope that it would match up with no overlapping and also with a total of 30 ECTS. This was really challenging

questions.question: Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer:
First I applied at Oslo University. Then I applied for courses at UNIS in October (the course registration deadline at UNIS was before getting an reply from Oslo University). For the course registration you could only apply for courses within the same department by prioritizing the courses in order. But since the courses were in different blocks and I wanted to register for several courses and from mixed departments, this was super confusing. So I had to e-mail UNIS and explain them my wishes in order to make it clear (it was just not possible through the course registration system). 

I applied for 5 courses and after some weeks I got answers from most of them. Most of them I was told I was disqualified while I got a waiting list spot on one course. So not enough to do the exchange at all. I e-mailed UNIS because I did not agree that I was disqualified and then they changed this so I got a spot in another course. But at this point I still only had 1 course of 10 ECTS, so I still needed two more. In my desperation I saw that the registration deadline was extended for a few courses, so I registered from one there and got a spot. Now I only  needed 1 more course, and the only thing i could do was to hope I would get a spot in the course I had a waiting list spot. On December 8 2023 I got the message that I was offered a spot through the waiting list and I accepted the offer. So only then I had enough courses to go on the ERASMUS exchange. So this was exactly 1 month before the semester started, so I had to fix equipment for high arctic, housing and flight tickets with very short time and this was super stressful.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: I could call and email UNIS.

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: Not super successful at first, but apparently, if you argument against the decline, you can change the decision. So in the end, I was pretty succesful with registering for the classes I wanted.

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer: If you do master exchange, good luck. It is super messy and stressful. My advice is to send motivation letter and maybe even a recommendation from your professor to succesfully register for the classes you want. UNIS say they dont want that, but apparently, people do this.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: Field activities are great, 10/10. But the in class course-activities were not great. The courses vary a lot in intensity and in learning outcome depending on who is running the course, so maybe ask previous students on opinions on the course before registering.

questions.question: Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: MA

questions.question: Did you take BA or MA courses at your host university? *
questions.answer: MA

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer: Not high, most people both BA and MA could have followed the courses

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer: Much more practical and much more fieldwork. Not a lot of reading and theory, but a lot of presentations, posters and discussions

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer: AB-329 Arctic Winter Ecology, AG-330 Permafrost and Periglacial Environments and AG-342 The Marine Cryosphere and its Cenozoic History

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: I would recommend Arctic Winter Ecology, the topics are super interesting and the professors are super motivated. I also partly recommend Permafrost and Periglacial Environments, since it is a super interesting topic, but our professors got sick so someone else took over the course with very short notice. Therefore, it was lacking some content and structure. The Marine Cryosphere and its Cenozoic History is also a super cool topic, but this was a very low intensity course with very little class activities, so I was a bit bored.

What unexpected costs did you encounter? *
questions.answer: I was on Svalbard in the spring semester, so snowscootering and skiing are super central activities. This is some serious expenses if you want to take part in this. But if you do exchange in Svalbard in the fall semester, this is none of your concern.

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer: Food is more expensive. Equipment is less expensive because there is a great second hand community in Longyearbyen and also the sports stores are tax free.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: There are great things such as kayaking and a sports hall with all sorts of sports such as swimming, climbing and so on.

questions.question: What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer: There are a few bars in town, and there is also a friday bar at UNIS.

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: I really enjoying doing outdoor activities, such as skiing, scootering and hiking. I highly recommend this since Svalbard has stunning nature.

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer: Outdoor activities with friends.

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: Super easy since the norwegian culture is close to danish culture

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer: No students are really local in UNIS

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: Norwegians are sometimes speaking norwegian even with internationals around. Also, they tend to socialize more with internationals when they drink alcohol and tend to be less extroverted e.g. in class

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: Norwegians are very happy with outdoor activities

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer:
Dont take a decline on course registration too serious, just explain why you think you are qualified and their decision might change 
Think about what you like to do in your free time when deciding if you go to svalbard in spring or summer season. If you like the extreme, scootering and skiing, you need more money but you will also have an amazing time. Be ready for fomo though! On the other hand, if these are not things you appreciate, choose the fall season, but be prepared that you are stuck in Longyearbyen with 2500 inhabitants and that you can more or less only get as far away from town as you can walk.

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer: Consider getting a norwegian D-number, bank ID and vipps as soon as possible. It makes your life a lot easier

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: Becoming more experienced regarding safety and outdoor activities and then doing more advanced stuff later in the semester. Also, feeling that my body got stronger and better at hiking.

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: To deal with the fomo and to find peace in a chaotic and socially intense student dorm

questions.question: Any other comments?
Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
